galaxy.title: The Milky Way
galaxy.subtitle: Left-drag to rotate · Scroll to zoom · Right-drag (or two fingers) to pan
galaxy.disclaimer: This model illustrates shape and scale; it is not a dynamical simulation. Stars are scattered along logarithmic spirals with random noise, and the true positions of the spiral arms are still being remeasured — the map of the galaxy has been redrawn several times in the past two decades. The figures in the table come from observation.

universe.title: The Universe
universe.subtitle: Drag to rotate · Scroll to zoom · The cosmic web at hundreds of millions of light-years
universe.scalesTitle: From the Milky Way to the cosmic horizon
universe.scalesIntro: Each step below is tens to hundreds of times larger than the one before. The shell radii in the model are compressed to fit the view — drawn to true scale, the Milky Way would be smaller than a pixel.
universe.disclaimer: This model reproduces the morphology of the cosmic web — filaments, nodes and voids — rather than simulating it: no gravity between dark matter halos is computed. Node positions are random and correspond to no real galaxy cluster. The figures in the table come from observation.
universe.fitsInView: At this scale you are seeing:
universe.tourHint: To fly from Earth out to the cosmic web, see the Zoom journey.

models.title: 3D models
models.subtitle: Three rungs of scale, each hundreds of thousands of times larger than the last
models.note: The three models are kept separate rather than merged into one continuously zoomable scene. The range of scale involved spans about 19 orders of magnitude, far beyond the precision of the 32-bit floats WebGL uses, so geometry would jitter if forced into a single scene. Each model is therefore tuned for its own scale, and they are linked by the scale ladder at the foot of each page.

zoom.title: The zoom journey
zoom.subtitle: Four levels, from the observable universe down to Earth
zoom.nextIsSmaller: The next level is about {factor}× smaller
zoom.note: Seven levels, seven separate scenes — not one continuously zoomable view. The four astronomical levels are 3D models; the continent level reuses the same Earth globe seen from close range, while the biology and human levels are illustrated with photographs because the project has no 3D assets for them. The span from the observable universe down to a human being is about 26 orders of magnitude, far beyond the precision of the 32-bit floats WebGL uses, so a single scene would fall apart. The seamless feel comes from zooming and cross-fading between adjacent levels.
